)
Join the Accelerator: Get 50% Off (
https://link.yudij.com/newsletteremail )
​
Before anything else, I want to say this.

I’m glad you’re here.

Still curious. Still trying. Still reading on January 1st.
That already tells me something about you.

This time of year is full of loud promises.
Big declarations. Big goals. Big energy.

But most meaningful change doesn’t start loudly.
It starts quietly, with a small decision to keep going.

I want this note to be that kind of beginning.

If you’re an international student or job seeker in the US (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/wvuvqz4n36ughk8z6r7b7hnq2okxxs8h6v89o/l2hehmhlwwp67mf6/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cueW91dHViZS5jb20vd2F0Y2g_dj04Rzl4ZjcxVm9Ncw==
), this year doesn’t just represent “new goals.”

It represents:
new chances
new timelines
new expectations
new pressure

And yet, also new learning.

Every conversation you had last year.
Every rejection that taught you what doesn’t work.
Every small win you didn’t celebrate enough.

None of that disappears because the calendar changed.

You’re not starting from zero.
You’re starting from experience.

One thing I’ve learned from working with students over the years
is this:

The people who do well aren’t the most confident on January 1st.
They’re the ones who stay consistent after January 15th.

They don’t try to overhaul everything.
They don’t chase motivation.
They build a rhythm they can return to even on heavy days.

That’s what I hope for you this year.
Not intensity. Not perfection.

Just steadiness.

If you’re job hunting, here’s a gentle way to think about the
months ahead.

Focus less on “breaking through”
and more on “showing up well.”

Clear roles.
Intentional applications.
Thoughtful conversations.
Enough rest to keep going.

Progress often looks boring while it’s happening.
That doesn’t make it meaningless.

This year doesn’t need a dramatic version of you.

It needs the same you,
a little clearer,
a little more patient,
a little more honest about what you want.

If you keep showing up with that energy, things move.
Sometimes slowly.
But they move.

I’m looking forward to walking this year with you.

Happy New Year.
The quiet, steady kind.

- Yudi J

The HireReady Newsletter Vol. 75: Infiltrating a Company by Solving Their Secret Problem

Forget the front door. The best opportunities aren't posted on job boards; they're hidden in plain sight, disguised as problems no one has had the courage or creativity to solve. This issue is about becoming the answer to a question a company doesn't even know it's asking. Stop applying for jobs and start creating them.

🛠️ The job search hacks 🛠️

🔍 Reverse-Engineer Their "Future You" with Jobscan's Resume Scanner 🔍

Everyone uses resume scanners (https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VWc8Fm2_TV2JV-tryp6BW-kXW4TqGZG5HNv_LN67vcnP3gP0xW7lCdLW6lZ3mKW99_K8N93Hr21W8PvQLW2_HyT6W4l0mR36C5d8SW9kSQHw8QMqGBW1_HW-F8wKH5dVvdLj52q-X-vW2ptqMW5TkHkcW9hj_mn5w5LHnW6p84SS2zjM6hW33wqQ36jNKwbW4Jwzrv44v1K6W9lkDSD7F17vpMLBW7Vq-k5BW5yTTJW4nwwCPW8vwskX7YTVTYW101RW13kpgp3W5F7tv78yCpFDW68j6Qf4JmfWVW2XbGpZ8DbHNpW2T9Jd05cBCG3W5wvtM-29zNcxW590HMF4MbsygW7jcFcV3pQd5kW4drX7V5jyf_Wf5Zx8h604 ) to match their resume to a current job description. That's playing checkers. I want you to play chess.

Instead of optimizing for the job they have open today, you're going to optimize for the job they'll need to create for you tomorrow. You'll do this by finding a job description for a role one or two levels above the one you're targeting at the same company or a direct competitor. This is the "future you" role. By scanning your resume against this more senior role, Jobscan (https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VWc8Fm2_TV2JV-tryp6BW-kXW4TqGZG5HNv_LN67vcnP3gP0xW7lCdLW6lZ3mKW99_K8N93Hr21W8PvQLW2_HyT6W4l0mR36C5d8SW9kSQHw8QMqGBW1_HW-F8wKH5dVvdLj52q-X-vW2ptqMW5TkHkcW9hj_mn5w5LHnW6p84SS2zjM6hW33wqQ36jNKwbW4Jwzrv44v1K6W9lkDSD7F17vpMLBW7Vq-k5BW5yTTJW4nwwCPW8vwskX7YTVTYW101RW13kpgp3W5F7tv78yCpFDW68j6Qf4JmfWVW2XbGpZ8DbHNpW2T9Jd05cBCG3W5wvtM-29zNcxW590HMF4MbsygW7jcFcV3pQd5kW4drX7V5jyf_Wf5Zx8h604 ) will reveal the precise skills and keywords you need to develop to become their ideal candidate for a promotion they haven't even thought of yet.

Next Steps:

- Find a job description for a role that is one or two promotions ahead of where you are now in your target company or a close competitor.
- Use Jobscan's Resume Scanner (https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VWc8Fm2_TV2JV-tryp6BW-kXW4TqGZG5HNv_LN67vcnP3gP0xW7lCdLW6lZ3mKW99_K8N93Hr21W8PvQLW2_HyT6W4l0mR36C5d8SW9kSQHw8QMqGBW1_HW-F8wKH5dVvdLj52q-X-vW2ptqMW5TkHkcW9hj_mn5w5LHnW6p84SS2zjM6hW33wqQ36jNKwbW4Jwzrv44v1K6W9lkDSD7F17vpMLBW7Vq-k5BW5yTTJW4nwwCPW8vwskX7YTVTYW101RW13kpgp3W5F7tv78yCpFDW68j6Qf4JmfWVW2XbGpZ8DbHNpW2T9Jd05cBCG3W5wvtM-29zNcxW590HMF4MbsygW7jcFcV3pQd5kW4drX7V5jyf_Wf5Zx8h604 ) to compare your current resume against this "future you" job description.
- Analyze the "missing skills" report not as a list of what you lack, but as your personal roadmap for professional development over the next six months.
- Begin strategically acquiring these skills and weaving them into your current projects and your LinkedIn profile.

Free Tool: Discover Future-Proof Skills
(https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VWc8Fm2_TV2JV-tryp6BW-kXW4TqGZG5HNv_LN67vcnP3gP0xW7lCdLW6lZ3mKW99_K8N93Hr21W8PvQLW2_HyT6W4l0mR36C5d8SW9kSQHw8QMqGBW1_HW-F8wKH5dVvdLj52q-X-vW2ptqMW5TkHkcW9hj_mn5w5LHnW6p84SS2zjM6hW33wqQ36jNKwbW4Jwzrv44v1K6W9lkDSD7F17vpMLBW7Vq-k5BW5yTTJW4nwwCPW8vwskX7YTVTYW101RW13kpgp3W5F7tv78yCpFDW68j6Qf4JmfWVW2XbGpZ8DbHNpW2T9Jd05cBCG3W5wvtM-29zNcxW590HMF4MbsygW7jcFcV3pQd5kW4drX7V5jyf_Wf5Zx8h604 )

💡 Become the Solution to Their Most Expensive Problem 💡

Companies are always trying to either make more money or save more money. Your mission is to figure out which expensive problem your target company is bleeding money on and present yourself as the solution. This isn't about finding a job opening; it's about finding a costly inefficiency.

Pour through their quarterly investor reports, read industry news about the challenges they're facing, and even look at customer complaints on social media. Is their customer churn too high? Are they spending a fortune on a particular software that isn't delivering? Find that financial pain point and build a simple, one-page proposal on how your skills could alleviate it.

Next Steps:

- Choose a target company and research their biggest financial and operational challenges.
- Identify a specific, high-cost problem that you have the skills to address.
- Draft a concise, one-page proposal that outlines the problem and your proposed solution, focusing on the potential cost savings or revenue generation.
- Identify the head of the department most affected by this problem and send them your proposal directly.

Guide: How to Show Your Value
(https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VWc8Fm2_TV2JV-tryp6BW-kXW4TqGZG5HNv_LN67vcp43gP0xW7Y8-PT6lZ3krW5-vCPX4FFjRfW4GsLfC3yNNBtW2zQfgr8KYbZCW2F289V2H3fkxW615DQt2jfqkyVZ3kTB4LXwVLMhzRyDhd2r9W6pMC3G4Bl05-W6Cj5_D5VMZWfW9bJxxy8tjJRFVGxg5x4-ZCfjW7hR3MR4DBJD5W7fwpSp4QGpGKN74w9LgPKMWRW42DSJR2-Myx2VQw7cf45t3P8N19KSN_8SSC-W6XcHfK38_hVxW35mqFQ10wWmBW6gQ8Xw2n49PsW4dnQK45h2L9HVWBY8q1bMd_NVplT2j3GJWrzW6khSLH7kK4LmW4tzjlW136716W7XBcY01C_d8Ff8-PZP804 )

🧠 The "Helpful Expert" LinkedIn Strategy 🧠

Stop networking and start helping. Instead of asking for a job, your goal is to become the most helpful person in your target company's professional network.

Identify key decision-makers and employees at the company on LinkedIn. Don't just connect and pitch; observe what they're posting about, what problems they're discussing, and what questions they're asking. Then, add real value to their conversations. Share a relevant article, offer a thoughtful perspective, or even create a short video explaining a solution to a problem they've mentioned. You're not a job seeker; you're a trusted expert who is already contributing to their success.

Next Steps:

- Identify 10-15 key people at your target company on LinkedIn.
- Follow their activity for a week and take notes on the challenges and topics they are discussing.
- Find or create a piece of content that directly addresses one of these challenges.
- Share this content in a comment on their post or in a brief, helpful direct message, with no expectation of anything in return.

(https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VWc8Fm2_TV2JV-tryp6BW-kXW4TqGZG5HNv_LN67vcp43gP0xW7Y8-PT6lZ3n6W6K099g5ZJ_P-W6_6VW76XhZj2VZ27vM1bNnvQW6C8ZVC3-H8t-N86_gybmfSX-W75QMnP6NLbNtW25gzqp8YQcDwW1x9k9p4B4gZVW6Tk_j05bSSnvW8ftzR93tFFsqW39pNx41jz60jW7-4hVB8jmYHwW7f3g4M8H0rn4W1mhfnS2sv3DnW5LcKSh443sLzW5FR2XD9b333DN9kd_lPt2N-tW6m5sFl90st1DW4R7TT58CNx3QVlqs2-3F9-ljW6qSnYG5ccDTnW4V2hb4783q86VBkxPZ5mS5VsW5D0Gst8FVx3qN6CVCcMCJkYqW3WhdfQ3GgGmSf2G_6wg04 )

📝 Conduct a "Pre-Interview" Project 📝

Why wait for them to give you a hypothetical interview question when you can solve a real problem for them right now? Identify a small but visible issue with your target company's product, service, or marketing. It could be a confusing part of their website, a gap in their social media content, or a customer service issue you've personally experienced. Create a small project that solves this problem. This could be a redesigned webpage mockup, a sample social media campaign, or a detailed customer feedback report with actionable suggestions. Send it to the relevant department head with a simple note: "I'm a huge fan of what you do, and I had a few ideas on how to make it even better."

Next Steps:

- Identify a small, specific, and solvable problem at your target company.
- Create a tangible solution. This could be a design, a written document, a short video, or a slide deck.
- Identify the person who is most likely responsible for the area you've addressed.
- Email them your project with a concise and enthusiastic message.

👥 The "Informational Interview" Reframe 👥

Everyone asks for an "informational interview" to learn about the company. Instead, you're going to request a "problem-solving session." When you reach out to someone at your target company, your ask will be different. "I've been following [Company Name]'s work in [specific area] and I have a few ideas that might help solve [a specific, well-researched problem]. Could I borrow 15 minutes of your time to walk you through them?"

This reframes you from a job seeker asking for a favor to a peer offering valuable insight. Even if your ideas aren't perfect, you've demonstrated initiative, creativity, and a genuine interest in helping them succeed.

Next Steps:

- Deeply research a challenge or opportunity at your target company.
- Develop 2-3 high-level, innovative ideas to address it.
- Identify the right person to share these ideas with.
- Send a concise email requesting a brief "problem-solving session" to share your thoughts.

🎯 A Smarter Job Search Strategy 🎯

If you’re still submitting the same resume to every job, you’re not alone, but it’s harder to stand out in today’s market. Career coach Elvi Caperonis recommends applying with intention, not urgency:

1️⃣ Tailor your resume to every role

Small adjustments in keywords, accomplishments, and phrasing can dramatically increase your match rate, and your chances of being seen.

2️⃣ Leverage LinkedIn to build genuine connections

Hiring is still human. Networking, thoughtful comments, and value-driven posts help you get on the radar before you even apply.

3️⃣ Know your strengths and use AI to find roles that truly fit

AI tools can help uncover hidden opportunities, improve keyword alignment, and identify roles that match your skills, not just your job title.

But the most important ingredient? A resilient mindset. “You may face rejections, but don’t take them personally… We are going to overcome them.”

In a world moving at the speed of AI—and soon, quantum—stability is no longer the goal. The most forward-thinking leaders aren’t searching for solid ground; they’re looking for the cracks where new opportunities will emerge. Our latest research highlights five data-driven trends that will define business leadership in 2026. Check them out below ⤵ 1️⃣ Uncertainty will be your greatest asset—if you embrace it In a volatile environment, rapid response is non-negotiable. In fact, 90% of executives say they’ll lose their edge if their organization can’t operate in real time. What to do → Rewire the organization for rapid response. 2️⃣ Employees will want more AI—not less There’s a perception gap at the heart of AI transformation. It's not just about automation—it’s about unlocking human potential. 61% of employees say AI makes their job less mundane and more strategic. Across all age groups, workers are increasingly open to deeper AI integration by their employers. What to do → Create a roadmap for roles that don’t yet exist. 👉 How will age groups respond to AI adoption in 2026? Two-thirds of consumers would switch brands if a company intentionally concealed AI’s involvement in their experience. 4️⃣ Global AI resilience will require a local safety net AI resilience hinges on uninterrupted access. That means AI sovereignty—an organization’s ability to control and govern its AI systems, data, and infrastructure at all times—has become mission-critical. What to do → Solidify your AI safeguards. 5️⃣ Quantum advantage will demand strength in numbers Quantum computing has moved well-beyond wishful thinking: Recent research indicates that quantum advantage is likely to emerge by the end of 2026. "USA is literally dead."

That’s the sentence I kept hearing during my recent India meetups
across four cities.
And honestly, I get why students feel this way.

The uncertainty.
Immigration noise.
Layoffs everywhere.
Stories of people struggling even after doing everything right.

After talking to hundreds of students face-to-face & in my
accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/mvugrxw8m6f5hqwxl5zcmhrk64lqqs3h26gnr/z2hghnhe0094v7up/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
), I realized something important.
People thinking about the US today fall into three very different
groups.

Group 1:​
They are clear. They have admits. They know why they are going.
Nothing shakes them.
If you are in this bucket, you are probably fine.

Group 2:​
They have already decided not to go.
They are tired of the drama and want to revisit the US later,
maybe 2028.
That choice is valid too.

Group 3:​
This is the group I worry about the most.

Ambitious.
Confused.
Smart.
Stuck between comfort in India and possibility in the US.

Some have work experience and a decent salary but wonder if they
are settling too early.
Others graduated recently, could not land a job, and see a US
master’s as their last hope.

If that’s you, this newsletter is for you.

A story you need to hear
------------------------

Let me tell you about someone I know. Let’s call him Vikram.

Middle-class background. Big dreams.
He believed hard work alone would figure everything out.

So he packed his bags and landed in the US with faith and
ambition.

What he did not expect was the reality.

Gatekeepers everywhere.
A brutal job market competing with laid-off engineers from Meta,
Amazon, Google.
No placements. No straight path.
Just networking, asking for chances, and constant uncertainty
around visas.

He eventually made it.
But the cost was emotional, financial, and mental.

And here’s the truth.
Most people land in the US without knowing what they are walking
into.

I don’t want that for you.

What I’ve observed after 100+ podcasts and 15 universities
----------------------------------------------------------

Some students landed jobs within 3- 4 months, even in the worst
job market.
Others are still struggling after a full year of OPT.

Luck matters. Timing matters.
But there are clear patterns.

Here are the three things students who made it had in common.

1. Career clarity (not vague dreams)
------------------------------------

"Tech."
"Management."
"AI something."

That’s not clarity. That’s confusion.

The students who succeeded knew:

* The exact role they were targeting
* What to type on LinkedIn
* The top companies hiring for that role
* Where alumni from their university worked
* And they started networking even before landing

If you don’t have this clarity, waiting is not failure. It’s
strategy.

2. Relentless focus
-------------------

These students were boring in the best way.

No constant partying.
No unnecessary drama.
They chose roommates carefully and protected their time.

They came for one reason and stayed loyal to it.

3. Realistic financial planning
-------------------------------

Many students are told, "On-campus jobs will cover everything."

That’s not always true.

On-campus jobs are limited. Competitive. Exhausting.

The smart students:

* Were strategic about on-campus work
* Avoided draining 20-hour labor jobs
* Preserved energy for internships, co-ops, and full-time roles

They understood why they were working, not just how much.

So, should you go to the US?
----------------------------

Ask yourself honestly:

* Do you have relevant or transferable work experience?
* Are you going to a university with real hiring outcomes?
* Are you okay with uncertainty and discomfort?
* If you lack experience, are you willing to go all-in from day
one?

If the answer feels fuzzy, pause.

Do not spend 50 lakhs to "find clarity."
Find clarity first. Then spend the money.

That’s how you get real ROI.

It’s a longer, honest conversation, and I think it will help you
think clearly instead of emotionally.

Get the latest from Amazon anytime by visiting About Amazon. As 2025 comes to a close, thank you for being part of the Amazon News community. Your engagement helps us share the stories behind the technologies and teams shaping Amazon’s future. This edition looks back at the AI breakthroughs that defined the year—from agentic systems and frontier models to smarter shopping, robotics, and global investments—and how they’re reshaping everyday experiences for customers, businesses, and communities heading into 2026. Amazon's AI innovations defining tomorrow For customers and businesses AI innovations transforming how people shop, sell, and experience Amazon How Amazon is using generative and agentic AI to transform the shopping experience Amazon is using generative and agentic AI—anchored by Rufus, our next-generation AI assistant for shopping, alongside tools like Buy for Me and AI-powered search and discovery—to help customers find, discover, and evaluate products from its broad selection more quickly and naturally, reducing the time and effort required to make confident purchase decisions. Read more → Scott Karpen, producer for 'Prime Vision with Next Gen Stats' Amazon's custom AI-powered Prime Insights take fans inside the game Prime Video introduced Prime Insights, a suite of AI-powered visual features including Defensive Alerts, Pressure Alert, Coverage ID, Prime Target, and Pocket Health that use real-time player tracking data and proprietary machine learning models to predict plays and highlight key moments across sports like Thursday Night Football, NASCAR, and the NBA. See inside → Amazon introduces agentic AI across the seller experience, transforming how sellers manage their businesses Powered by Amazon Bedrock, Seller Assistant evolves into an always-on, agentic AI-powered partner that helps sellers launch, manage, and grow their business, handling everything from routine operations to complex business strategy while keeping sellers in control. Read more → Amazon unveils the next generation of AI-powered Echo devices, purpose-built for Alexa+ Amazon announced four new Echo devices built from the ground up for Alexa+, powered by custom-designed silicon, Omnisense sensor fusion, and next-generation AI processing. Together, these advances enable more personalized, proactive, and deeply conversational Alexa+ experiences that fade into the background of everyday life, making the new Echo lineup the best way for customers to experience Alexa+ out of the box. Read more → Amazon SVP of Devices and Services Panos Panay on the future of AI devices: For developers and enterprise AI tools and infrastructure powering the next generation of innovation AWS unveils frontier agents, a new class of AI agents that work as an extension of your software development team The first three frontier agents—Kiro autonomous agent, AWS Security Agent, and AWS DevOps Agent—are autonomous, scalable, and work independently for hours or days without constant intervention, revolutionizing how teams build, secure, and operate software by functioning as extensions of development teams rather than just task assistants. Read more → Meet Amazon Quick Suite: The agentic AI application reshaping how work gets done QuickSuite answers questions and gets detailed answers, conducts deep dive research, analyzes and visualizes data, and creates automations for workflows across all your information with enterprise-grade security and privacy standards, transforming tasks that used to take days into minutes while connecting to over 50 built-in applications and 1,000+ apps through integrations. Read more → Inside an AWS Trainium chip. A city in the palm of your hand: Exploring the intricate world of an Amazon Web Services Trainium chip Tour the micro metropolis where calculations run 24/7 and data commutes at light speed—AWS Trainium is a custom-designed AI chip that completes trillions of calculations a second, with 64 interconnected chips working in concert to power one of the world's most powerful computers for training AI. See inside → Amazon introduces new frontier Nova models, a pioneering Nova Forge service for organizations to build their own models, and Nova Act for building agents Nova 2 models deliver industry-leading price-performance across reasoning, multimodal processing, conversational AI, code generation, and agentic tasks, while Nova Forge pioneers "open training" that empowers organizations to build their own optimized model variants by blending proprietary data with Nova's frontier capabilities, and Nova Act achieves breakthrough 90% reliability for browser-based UI automation workflows. ​
"USA is literally dead."

That’s the sentence I kept hearing during my recent India meetups
across four cities.
And honestly, I get why students feel this way.

The uncertainty.
Immigration noise.
Layoffs everywhere.
Stories of people struggling even after doing everything right.

After talking to hundreds of students face-to-face & in my
accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/n4uq7w9026hvhxelep0a6h68xz5ggflhew90n/kkhmh6hn4696qdhl/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
), I realized something important.
People thinking about the US today fall into three very different
groups.

Group 1:​
They are clear. They have admits. They know why they are going.
Nothing shakes them.
If you are in this bucket, you are probably fine.

Group 2:​
They have already decided not to go.
They are tired of the drama and want to revisit the US later,
maybe 2028.
That choice is valid too.

Group 3:​
This is the group I worry about the most.

Ambitious.
Confused.
Smart.
Stuck between comfort in India and possibility in the US.

Some have work experience and a decent salary but wonder if they
are settling too early.
Others graduated recently, could not land a job, and see a US
master’s as their last hope.

If that’s you, this newsletter is for you.

A story you need to hear
------------------------

Let me tell you about someone I know. Let’s call him Vikram.

Middle-class background. Big dreams.
He believed hard work alone would figure everything out.

So he packed his bags and landed in the US with faith and
ambition.

What he did not expect was the reality.

Gatekeepers everywhere.
A brutal job market competing with laid-off engineers from Meta,
Amazon, Google.
No placements. No straight path.
Just networking, asking for chances, and constant uncertainty
around visas.

He eventually made it.
But the cost was emotional, financial, and mental.

And here’s the truth.
Most people land in the US without knowing what they are walking
into.

I don’t want that for you.

What I’ve observed after 100+ podcasts and 15 universities
----------------------------------------------------------

Some students landed jobs within 3- 4 months, even in the worst
job market.
Others are still struggling after a full year of OPT.

Luck matters. Timing matters.
But there are clear patterns.

Here are the three things students who made it had in common.

1. Career clarity (not vague dreams)
------------------------------------

"Tech."
"Management."
"AI something."

That’s not clarity. That’s confusion.

The students who succeeded knew:

* The exact role they were targeting
* What to type on LinkedIn
* The top companies hiring for that role
* Where alumni from their university worked
* And they started networking even before landing

If you don’t have this clarity, waiting is not failure. It’s
strategy.

2. Relentless focus
-------------------

These students were boring in the best way.

No constant partying.
No unnecessary drama.
They chose roommates carefully and protected their time.

They came for one reason and stayed loyal to it.

3. Realistic financial planning
-------------------------------

Many students are told, "On-campus jobs will cover everything."

That’s not always true.

On-campus jobs are limited. Competitive. Exhausting.

The smart students:

* Were strategic about on-campus work
* Avoided draining 20-hour labor jobs
* Preserved energy for internships, co-ops, and full-time roles

They understood why they were working, not just how much.

So, should you go to the US?
----------------------------

Ask yourself honestly:

* Do you have relevant or transferable work experience?
* Are you going to a university with real hiring outcomes?
* Are you okay with uncertainty and discomfort?
* If you lack experience, are you willing to go all-in from day
one?

If the answer feels fuzzy, pause.

Do not spend 50 lakhs to "find clarity."
Find clarity first. Then spend the money.

That’s how you get real ROI.

It’s a longer, honest conversation, and I think it will help you
think clearly instead of emotionally.

One pattern I keep noticing after talking to hundreds of
international students and job seekers is this:

Most people struggling in the U.S. job market are not lazy.
They’re not under-skilled.
They’re not careless.

They’re just playing the game without fully understanding how it
works.

And the U.S. job market is very much a game of rules.

When students land in the U.S., the focus usually goes here:

* getting good grades
* doing more projects
* adding certifications
* "working harder" than everyone else

All of that feels productive.
But it doesn’t always translate into interviews or offers.

I’ve seen people with average resumes land roles quickly.
And others with strong profiles struggle for months.

The difference is rarely effort.
It’s timing, positioning, and how early they start.

A pattern I see again and again
-------------------------------

Some job seekers prepare before they land.
Others wait until things "settle down."

The first group usually:

* has a resume ready
* knows which roles they’re targeting
* understands what companies actually look for
* starts applying immediately

The second group:

* spends the first 1–2 months adjusting
* figures things out slowly
* applies late
* feels behind before they even start

Both groups may work equally hard.
But their outcomes look very different.

That early preparation creates momentum.
And momentum changes everything.

Another pattern that shows up often
-----------------------------------

Some job seekers wait to feel "ready."
Others move even when things feel uncomfortable.

The ones who move early:

* apply even when their resume isn’t perfect
* talk to people instead of waiting for job boards
* show up at events, offices, or meetups
* learn on the job instead of waiting to know everything

They don’t wait for permission.
They put themselves in rooms where opportunities exist.

Their resumes don’t magically improve overnight.
But their exposure does.

And exposure leads to interviews.

The uncomfortable truth
-----------------------

In the U.S. job market:

* effort is invisible
* intentions don’t matter
* preparation beats talent
* speed beats perfection

Recruiters don’t see how stressed you are.
They only see what you show up with when the opportunity appears.

That’s why people who prepare early often look "lucky" later.

If you’re job hunting right now
-------------------------------

Instead of asking:
"Am I good enough?"

Try asking:

* Am I applying early or late?
* Do I clearly know which role I’m targeting?
* Does my resume show impact or just activity?
* Am I talking to people or only clicking apply?
* If an interview comes tomorrow, am I ready?

These questions move the needle more than one more project.

If you’re already working in the U.S.
-------------------------------------

This still applies.

Layoffs, visa pressure, and team instability are realities.
A big company name alone won’t protect you.

What helps is:

* owning problems that matter
* understanding how your work ties to revenue or risk
* keeping your network warm even when things feel stable
* preparing before you need to job hunt again

The people who recover fastest from layoffs usually started
preparing long before the layoff.

One last thing-

The U.S. job market doesn’t reward effort.
It rewards timing, positioning, and consistency.

Once you understand that, the anxiety reduces.
Because now you’re playing the right game.

And if you ever feel like you’re doing a lot but going nowhere,
that’s usually not a motivation issue.
It’s a structure issue.

).
No hype. No shortcuts. Just systems that work for international
students.

By Tushar Sahu


By Tushar Sahu

    
    
    Read this article on LinkedIn to join the conversation

https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/from-salary-ceiling-unlimited-growth-why-smart-people-tushar-sahu-aqlwc?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_01%3BN0VcsktoQWeEyyWfUIP%2BWg%3D%3D&midToken=AQEIM4HzHiyK2w&midSig=2k4lqffPOnlc41&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_01-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_01-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-ghmp60~mjoafgjd~ks-null-null&eid=ghmp60-mjoafgjd-ks&otpToken=MWIwYzE5ZTAxNTJmY2FjN2IyMjQwNGVkNDAxOGVmYjc4NmNmZDg0MTlhYTg4YjYxNzljNDA3NmI0YjU5NWZmYWY3ZDFkZjk5NjliOWVkZmE3Mjg2ZDA4NDk3MWEwMjg4ZThhMWU1NWYxOTkxNjEzYWE0ZTVhZiwxLDE%3D
  
The Path Less Traveled That Leads to Extraordinary Growth In a world where most pursue the safety of a 9-to-5, entrepreneurship stands as a beacon for those craving autonomy, impact, and exponential growth. Whether you're a student, professional, or someone at a crossroads, here's why building your own venture might be your calling. 1. FREEDOM TO DEFINE YOUR OWN RULES As an entrepreneur, you're not bound by corporate hierarchies or someone else's vision. You set the roadmap. You decide what gets built, how it's built, and who you work with. This autonomy is liberating—and it's what drives relentless execution. 2. UNLIMITED INCOME POTENTIAL Your salary cap is only your ambition. In employment, there's a ceiling. As an entrepreneur? Your income scales with your business's growth. I've witnessed businesses that started with zero capital generating 6-7 figures in months. That's the power of compounding effort and smart systems. 3. SKILL ACCELERATION LIKE NOTHING ELSE Nothing teaches you faster than real money on the line. You'll learn marketing, sales, finance, operations, and product development—not from textbooks, but through execution. Every mistake becomes a lesson. Every win builds confidence. 4. IMPACT THAT COMPOUNDS Your job serves your employer's vision. Your business serves your vision and impacts customers directly. Building something meaningful—whether it's a SaaS product, lead generation platform, or content brand—creates ripple effects far beyond your own income. 5. BUILD VALUABLE CONNECTIONS Entrepreneurs surround themselves with other builders. You'll form deeper relationships with mentors, peers, and investors. These networks often become more valuable than the business itself. 6. TAX EFFICIENCY & WEALTH BUILDING Businesses have legitimate tax advantages individuals don't have. Expense deductions, equity appreciation, and asset building are game-changers for long-term wealth creation. 7. YOU OWN THE UPSIDE In employment, shareholders own your value creation. As an entrepreneur, every dollar of growth belongs to you (and your team). That equity compounds into generational wealth. THE REAL TRUTH Entrepreneurship isn't for everyone—and that's okay. It requires relentless discipline, tolerance for risk, and acceptance of uncertainty. You'll work harder than ever before. You'll face rejection, failure, and doubt. But if you have something to build, a problem to solve, or a vision that won't leave you alone... then entrepreneurship isn't a choice. It's a necessity. The question isn't "Should I become an entrepreneur?" The question is: "Can I afford NOT to?" Start today. Start small. Start now.

Founder Tip: Every engineer graduating now should join a startup first.

Kartik Hegde <https://www.linkedin.com/in/kartikhegde/>, CEO of ChipStack 
<https://www.chipstack.ai/>, flips the usual advice. Some treat startups as the 
risky move you make after you've "figured it out" at a big company.

Early career is when you can afford to fail. Startups give you direct impact 
and no buffer between you and the problem. The corporate path teaches you to 
optimize inside someone else's system. Startups teach you whether you can build 
one.

It's easier to transition from a startup to a corporate setting than the 
reverse. Big companies will hire someone who's learned to operate without 
structure. Startups want people who've already done it.

Job Search Tip: What AI can't replace in your career.

Jassi Starleaf <https://www.linkedin.com/in/jassistarleaf/>, Senior Technical 
Recruiter atQuillbot <https://quillbot.com/>, answers "Will AI replace 
entry-level jobs?"

 AI won't replace your social and emotional intelligence. It won't replace 
complex problem solving, critical thinking, or creativity. What it will expose 
is who's been coasting on repetitive tasks.

The play isn't to avoid AI; it's to show you can work with it. Use it to 
brainstorm, then lead with judgment. Mention AI in your project examples, but 
highlight the human decisions that mattered.

The Monthly AI Recap

By Google


By Google

Read on LinkedIn

This article was written by Jeff Dean, Chief Scientist, Demis Hassabis, CEO Google DeepMind and James Manyika, SVP Research, Labs, Technology & Society. 2025 has been a year of extraordinary progress in research. With artificial intelligence, we can see its trajectory shifting from a tool to a utility: from something people use to something they can put to work. If 2024 was about laying the multimodal foundations for this era, 2025 was the year AI began to really think, act and explore the world alongside us. With quantum computing, we made progress towards real-world applications. And across the board, we helped turn research into reality, with more capable and useful products and tools making a positive impact on people's lives today. Here’s a look back at some of the breakthroughs, products and scientific milestones that defined the work of Google, Google DeepMind and Google Research in a year of relentless progress. Delivering breakthroughs on world-class models This year, we significantly advanced our model capabilities with breakthroughs on reasoning, multimodal understanding, model efficiency, and generative capabilities, beginning with the release of Gemini 2.5 in March and culminating in the November launch of Gemini 3 and the December launch of Gemini 3 Flash. Built on a foundation of state-of-the-art reasoning, Gemini 3 Pro is our most powerful model to date, designed to help you bring any idea to life. It topped the LMArena Leaderboard and redefined multimodal reasoning with breakthrough scores on benchmarks like Humanity’s Last Exam — a fiendishly hard test for AI models to see if AI can truly think and reason like humans — and GPQA Diamond. It also set a new standard for frontier models in mathematics, achieving a new state-of-the-art of 23.4% on MathArena Apex. We followed shortly with Gemini 3 Flash, which combines Gemini 3's Pro-grade reasoning with Flash-level latency, efficiency and cost, making it the most performant model for its size. Gemini 3 Flash's quality surpasses our previous Gemini 2.5 Pro-scale model's capabilities at a fraction of the price and substantially better latency, continuing our Gemini-era trend of 'the next generation's Flash model is better than the previous generation's Pro model'. Learn more about our progress on our world-class AI models this year: Gemini 3 Flash: frontier intelligence built for speed (Dec 2025) A new era of intelligence with Gemini 3 (Nov 2025) Introducing Nano Banana Pro (Nov 2025) Introducing Veo 3.1 and new creative capabilities in the Gemini API (Nov 2025) Gemini 2.5: Our most intelligent AI model (March 2025) Gemini 3 Flash price & benchmark table. We’re committed to making useful AI technology accessible, with state-of-the-art open models. We built our Gemma family of models to be lightweight and open for public use; this year we were able to introduce multimodal capabilities, significantly increase the context window, expand multilingual capabilities, and improve efficiency and performance. Learn more about this year’s advances in Gemma models: Introducing Gemma 3: The most capable model you can run on a single GPU or TPU (March 2025) Introducing Gemma 3 270M: The compact model for hyper-efficient AI (Aug 2025) Innovating and transforming our products with AI Throughout 2025, we continued to advance the trajectory of AI from tool to utility, transforming our portfolio of products with new, powerful agentic capabilities. We reimagined software development by moving beyond tools that assist coding to introducing powerful, agentic systems that collaborate with developers. Key advances, such as the impressive coding capabilities in Gemini 3 and the launch of Google Antigravity, mark a new era in AI-assisted software development. Learn more about this year’s advances building developer tools: Start building with Gemini 3 (Nov 2025) Introducing Google Antigravity, a New Era in AI-Assisted Software Development (Nov 2025) This evolution was also clear across our core products, from AI-enabled features on the Pixel 10 and updates to AI Mode in Search, to AI-first innovations like the Gemini app and NotebookLM, which gained advanced features like Deep Research. Learn more about how we’ve transformed our products with AI: 9 ways AI makes Pixel 10 our most helpful phone yet (Aug 2025) Expanding AI Overviews and introducing AI Mode (March 2025) Gemini 3 brings upgraded smarts and new capabilities to the Gemini app (Nov 2025) NotebookLM adds Deep Research and support for more source types (Nov 2025) Empowering creativity and co-creating with AI 2025 was a transformative year for generative media, giving people new and unprecedented capabilities to realize their creative ambitions. Generative media models and tools for video, images, audio and worlds became more effective and broadly used, with breakouts Nano Banana and Nano Banana Pro offering unprecedented capabilities for native image generation and editing. We worked with people in creative industries to develop tools like Flow and Music AI Sandbox, making them more helpful for creative workflows, and we expanded creative possibilities for people with new, AI-powered experiences in the Google Arts & Culture lab, major upgrades to image editing within the Gemini app, and the introduction of powerful new generative media models like Veo 3.1, Imagen 4 and Flow. Learn more about how we’re building AI to enhance creativity: Art, science, travel: 3 new AI-powered experiences this holiday season (Nov 2025) Introducing Veo 3.1 and advanced capabilities in Flow (Oct 2025) Nano Banana: Image editing in Gemini just got a major upgrade (Aug 2025) Veo 3, Imagen 4, and Flow: Fuel your creativity with new generative media models and tools (May 2025) Music AI Sandbox, now with new features and broader access (April 2025) As research breakthroughs continue to expand AI’s capabilities, Google Labs is where we share AI experiments as we develop them — hearing from users and evolving as we learn. Some of this year’s most engaging experiments from Labs: Pomelli, an AI experiment for on-brand marketing content; Stitch, which introduced a way to turn prompt and image inputs into complex UI designs and frontend code in minutes; Jules, an asynchronous coding agent that acts as a collaborative partner for developers; and Google Beam, a 3D video communications platform that used AI to advance the possibilities of remote presence. Learn more about how we’re experimenting in Labs: Create on-brand marketing content for your business with Pomelli (Oct 2025) Google Beam: Our AI-first 3D video communication platform (May 2025) From idea to app: Introducing Stitch, a new way to design UIs (May 2025) Build with Jules, your asynchronous coding agent (May 2025) Advancing science and mathematics 2025 was also a banner year for scientific advances with AI, marked by breakthroughs in life sciences, health, natural sciences, and mathematics. In the space of a year, we made progress in building AI resources and tools that empower researchers and help them understand, identify, and develop treatments in healthcare. In genomics, where we’ve been applying advanced technology to research for 10 years, we moved beyond sequencing, using AI to interpret the most complex data. We also marked the 5-year anniversary of AlphaFold, the Nobel-winning AI system that solved the 50-year-old protein folding problem. AlphaFold has been used by over 3 million researchers in more than 190 countries, including over 1 million users in low- and middle-income countries. Learn more about how we’re using AI to advance life sciences and health: AlphaFold: Five years of impact (Nov 2025) Using AI to identify genetic variants in tumors with DeepSomatic (Oct 2025) AI as a research partner: Advancing theoretical computer science with AlphaEvolve (Sept 2025) AlphaGenome: AI for better understanding the genome (June 2025) Accelerating scientific breakthroughs with an AI co-scientist (Feb 2025) Gemini’s advanced thinking capabilities, including Deep Think, also enabled historic progress in mathematics and coding. Deep Think was able to solve problems that require deep abstract reasoning — achieving gold medal-standard in two international contests. Learn more about how we’re advancing natural sciences and mathematics: Gemini achieves gold-medal level at the International Collegiate Programming Contest World Finals (Sept 2025) Advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think officially achieves gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad (July 2025) Shaping innovations in computing and the physical world We’re also leading major discoveries and shaping the future of science in areas like quantum computing, energy and moonshots. Research in this area drew new levels of public attention, with progress towards real-world applications of quantum computing as demonstrated by Quantum Echoes and, notably, Googler Michel Devoret becoming a 2025 Physics Nobel Laureate along with former Googler John Martinis and UC Berkeley’s John Clarke, for their foundational 1980s quantum research. Learn more about our work on space infrastructure and quantum computing: Project Suncatcher: Exploring a space-based, scalable AI infrastructure system design (Nov 2025) Googler Michel Devoret awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (Oct 2025) Our Quantum Echoes algorithm is a big step toward real-world applications for quantum computing (Oct 2025) In 2025, we continued to advance the core infrastructure that powers our AI, focusing on breakthroughs in hardware design and improving energy efficiency. This included the introduction of Ironwood, a new TPU built for the age of inference, which was designed using a method called AlphaChip, alongside a commitment to measuring the environmental impact of our technology. Learn more about how we’re using AI to develop chips, infrastructure and improve energy efficiency: 3 things to know about Ironwood, our latest TPU (Nov 2025) How much energy does Google’s AI use? We did the math (Aug 2025) Ironwood: The first Google TPU for the age of inference (April 2025) Our work in robotics and visual understanding brought AI agents into both the physical and virtual worlds, with advancements like the foundational Gemini Robotics models, the more sophisticated Gemini Robotics 1.5, and the introduction of Genie 3 as a new frontier for general-purpose world models. Learn more about our work with world models and robotics: Gemini Robotics 1.5 brings AI agents into the physical world (Sept 2025) Genie 3: A new frontier for world models (Aug 2025) Gemini Robotics brings AI into the physical world (March 2025) Tackling global challenges and opportunities at scale Our work throughout 2025 demonstrates how AI-enabled scientific progress is being directly applied to address the world's most critical and pervasive challenges. By leveraging state-of-the-art foundational models and agentic reasoning, we are significantly increasing our understanding of the planet and its systems, while also delivering impactful solutions in areas vital to human flourishing, including climate resilience, public health and education. For example, we are using state-of-the-art foundational models and agentic reasoning to help increase our understanding of the planet, helping enable work that is making a difference in people’s lives now from weather predictions to urban planning to public health. For example, our flood forecasting information now covers more than two billion people in 150 countries for severe riverine floods. And our most advanced and efficient forecasting model, WeatherNext 2 can generate forecasts 8x faster and with resolution up to 1-hour. Using this technology, we’ve supported weather agencies in making decisions based on a range of scenarios through our experimental cyclone predictions. Learn more about our work in weather, mapping and wildfires: WeatherNext 2: Our most advanced weather forecasting model (Nov 2025) New updates and more access to Google Earth AI (Oct 2025) Google Earth AI: Our state-of-the-art geospatial AI models (July 2025) AlphaEarth Foundations helps map our planet in unprecedented detail (July 2025) How we're supporting better tropical cyclone prediction with AI (June 2025) Inside the launch of FireSat, a system to find wildfires earlier (March 2025) We are working with partners to apply AI-enabled scientific progress closer to patients, opening up new avenues for disease management and therapeutic discovery. Learn more about our health-related work: Cell2Sentence-Scale 27B: How a Gemma model helped discover a new potential cancer therapy pathway (Oct 2025) From diagnosis to treatment: Advancing AMIE for longitudinal disease management (March 2025) AI is proving to be a powerful tool in education, enabling new forms of understanding and expanding curiosity through initiatives like LearnLM and Guided Learning in Gemini. We brought Gemini’s most powerful translation capabilities to Google Translate, enabling much smarter, more natural and accurate translations and piloting new speech to speech translation capabilities. Learn more about how we’re using AI to enable learning: Bringing state-of-the-art Gemini translation capabilities to Google Translate (Dec 2025) Guided Learning in Gemini: From answers to understanding (Aug 2025) How generative AI expands curiosity and understanding with LearnLM (May 2025) Prioritizing responsibility and safety We couple our research breakthroughs with rigorous and forward-looking work on responsibility and safety. As our models grow more capable, we’re continuing to advance and evolve our tools, resources and safety frameworks to anticipate and mitigate risk. Gemini 3 demonstrated this approach in action: it's our most secure model yet, and has undergone the most comprehensive set of safety evaluations of any Google AI model to date. And we’re looking further ahead, exploring a responsible path to AGI, prioritizing readiness, proactive risk assessment, and collaboration with the wider AI community. Learn more about our responsibility and safety work: You can now verify Google AI-generated videos in the Gemini app (Dec 2025) How we’re bringing AI image verification to the Gemini app (Nov 2025) Strengthening our Frontier Safety Framework (September 2025) Taking a responsible path to AGI (April 2025) Evaluating potential cybersecurity threats of advanced AI (April 2025) Leading frontier collaborations with industry, academia and civil society Advancing the frontier of AI responsibly demands collaboration across all parts of society. In 2025, we worked with leading AI labs to help to form the Agentic AI Foundation and support open standards to ensure a responsible and interoperable future for agentic AI. In education, we’ve partnered with school districts like Miami Dade County and education groups like Raspberry Pi to equip students with AI skills. Our research partnerships with universities like UC Berkeley, Yale, the University of Chicago and many more have been instrumental to some of this year’s most exciting frontier research, and we’re working with the US Department of Energy’s 17 national laboratories to transform how scientific research is conducted. And we’re working with filmmakers and other creative visionaries to put the best AI tools in their hands and explore storytelling in the age of AI. Learn more about our work on frontier collaboration: Google DeepMind supports U.S. Department of Energy on Genesis: a national mission to accelerate innovation and scientific discovery (Dec 2025) Formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), Anchored by New Project Contributions Including Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose and AGENTS.md (Dec 2025) Announcing Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for Google services (Dec 2025) Our latest commitments in AI and learning (Nov 2025) Partnering to power Miami’s AI-ready future (Oct 2025) AI on Screen premiere: “Sweetwater” short film explores new AI narratives (Sept 2025) Behind “ANCESTRA”: combining Veo with live-action filmmaking (Jun 2025) How Indian music legend Shankar Mahadevan experiments with Music AI Sandbox (April 2025) Looking ahead As we look towards 2026, we’re looking forward to continuing to advance the frontier, safely and responsibly, for the benefit of humanity.

One pattern I keep noticing after talking to hundreds of
international students and job seekers is this:

Most people struggling in the U.S. job market are not lazy.
They’re not under-skilled.
They’re not careless.

They’re just playing the game without fully understanding how it
works.

And the U.S. job market is very much a game of rules.

When students land in the U.S., the focus usually goes here:

* getting good grades
* doing more projects
* adding certifications
* "working harder" than everyone else

All of that feels productive.
But it doesn’t always translate into interviews or offers.

I’ve seen people with average resumes land roles quickly.
And others with strong profiles struggle for months.

The difference is rarely effort.
It’s timing, positioning, and how early they start.

A pattern I see again and again
-------------------------------

Some job seekers prepare before they land.
Others wait until things "settle down."

The first group usually:

* has a resume ready
* knows which roles they’re targeting
* understands what companies actually look for
* starts applying immediately

The second group:

* spends the first 1–2 months adjusting
* figures things out slowly
* applies late
* feels behind before they even start

Both groups may work equally hard.
But their outcomes look very different.

That early preparation creates momentum.
And momentum changes everything.

Another pattern that shows up often
-----------------------------------

Some job seekers wait to feel "ready."
Others move even when things feel uncomfortable.

The ones who move early:

* apply even when their resume isn’t perfect
* talk to people instead of waiting for job boards
* show up at events, offices, or meetups
* learn on the job instead of waiting to know everything

They don’t wait for permission.
They put themselves in rooms where opportunities exist.

Their resumes don’t magically improve overnight.
But their exposure does.

And exposure leads to interviews.

The uncomfortable truth
-----------------------

In the U.S. job market:

* effort is invisible
* intentions don’t matter
* preparation beats talent
* speed beats perfection

Recruiters don’t see how stressed you are.
They only see what you show up with when the opportunity appears.

That’s why people who prepare early often look "lucky" later.

If you’re job hunting right now
-------------------------------

Instead of asking:
"Am I good enough?"

Try asking:

* Am I applying early or late?
* Do I clearly know which role I’m targeting?
* Does my resume show impact or just activity?
* Am I talking to people or only clicking apply?
* If an interview comes tomorrow, am I ready?

These questions move the needle more than one more project.

If you’re already working in the U.S.
-------------------------------------

This still applies.

Layoffs, visa pressure, and team instability are realities.
A big company name alone won’t protect you.

What helps is:

* owning problems that matter
* understanding how your work ties to revenue or risk
* keeping your network warm even when things feel stable
* preparing before you need to job hunt again

The people who recover fastest from layoffs usually started
preparing long before the layoff.

One last thing-

The U.S. job market doesn’t reward effort.
It rewards timing, positioning, and consistency.

Once you understand that, the anxiety reduces.
Because now you’re playing the right game.

And if you ever feel like you’re doing a lot but going nowhere,
that’s usually not a motivation issue.
It’s a structure issue.

No hype. No shortcuts. Just systems that work for international

I’ve personally used Crobo for over a year. What I like is simple

)
Give it a try -> Crobo Money (
https://crobo.onelink.me/RNBj/YUDI_NY_NL )
​
I just wrapped a podcast that honestly left me sitting quietly in
the studio for a few minutes.

You can watch it here → Link (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/5quzwk28xph7hnldedeu6h9286v44bnhrvn8m/48hvhehmk260n5fx/aHR0cHM6Ly95b3V0dS5iZS9ILUJKM08xLVhOYw==
)​

Because listening to Riya felt like watching the hidden journey
of thousands of international students.

The part no consultant back home prepares you for.
The part your parents never hear about because you don’t want to
worry them.

And the part you quietly fight alone.

When she said,
​"I didn’t feel enough… I felt guilty I was spending my father’s
money."​
It shook me.

She came to the U.S. confident, ambitious, thinking she would
figure things out quickly.
Within weeks, reality hit her hard.
Rejections.
Silent applications.
Resume tears.
Friends getting interviews, she didn’t.
And that terrible mix of self-doubt and pressure that only
international students truly understand.

But here’s what made her story powerful.
She didn’t stay in that place.

The turning point
-----------------

At one point, she said she was applying everywhere with one
generic resume.
No strategy. No alignment. Just panic.

Then something snapped.
Her batchmates - the right ones - sat her down and told her the
truth:

"You’re applying wrong. Fix your resume. Apply within 24 hours.
Match the keywords.
Stop scrolling Instagram on the bus. Start scrolling LinkedIn."

It stung, but it changed everything.

And then something even bigger happened.
She went for a resume review with Purdue MEM’s career advisor,
Katie… and she broke down crying.
Because she finally saw how far behind she felt.
Katie didn’t judge her. She hugged her. She walked her through
what to fix.
She reminded her she belonged here.

That moment gave her the confidence to rebuild.

This is what makes Purdue MEM (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/5quzwk28xph7hnldedeu6h9286v44bnhrvn8m/wnh2hghq8oxr3kc7/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9wdXJkdWVtZW0=
)special - not just the coursework, but the humans behind it,
guiding you through the toughest phase of your career.

You can explore Purdue MEM program here (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/5quzwk28xph7hnldedeu6h9286v44bnhrvn8m/wnh2hghq8oxr3kc7/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9wdXJkdWVtZW0=
).

From chaos to clarity
---------------------

Once she learned how to structure her resume, research roles,
target companies that sponsor, and ask for referrals properly…
everything shifted.

She wasn’t doing "more."
She was finally doing what mattered.

That’s when the interview calls started coming - TikTok,
automotive companies, and eventually Tesla.​
Not because of luck, but because she learned how to think
strategically:

• match your resume to the job
• apply early
• use keywords
• ask seniors for feedback
• understand what companies actually need
• stay honest in interviews
• follow up properly with thank you emails and answers you missed

This is the exact transformation most international students in
my Accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/5quzwk28xph7hnldedeu6h9286v44bnhrvn8m/reh8hohmn5wqe7c2/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
) go through - from panic mode to structured strategy.

Because behind every internship or offer is a journey your
LinkedIn feed never shows.
The tears. The family pressure.
The moments you question your worth.
The loneliness of being in a foreign country with no one to tell
you what’s right or wrong.

And yet… the students who make it are the ones who learn to
rebuild themselves like Riya did.
One strategy at a time.
One conversation at a time.
One tough day at a time.

Her story isn’t just inspiring.
It’s a mirror for so many of you.

If you’re going through something similar, I hope you listen to
this conversation.

It’ll give you perspective, strategy, and maybe a bit of hope

Your Elastic Observability trial is ready to work for you — all it needs is your data.

By Abhishek Kumar


By Abhishek Kumar

A short story about pointers, memory, and why returning &value should make your nose wrinkle Let me show you a program. Read it carefully. Answer honestly. Alice lives in London. Bob lives in London. Both were set from the exact same constant — LONDON. Are their cities equal? ... The program prints false. Wait. What? I know. Your brain screamed "true". Mine did too. Here's the thing: City() doesn't return a City. It returns a *City — a pointer to a City. A memory address. And when you compare two pointers with ==, Go doesn't ask "do these point to the same value?" It asks "are these the exact same address in memory?" Alice and Bob are two separate Person structs living in two separate places in memory. Alice's city field lives at, say, address 0xc0000b4010. Bob's city field lives at 0xc0000b4030. Different houses. Different addresses. Even though both houses have "London" written on the door. The contents are identical. The addresses are not. And == on pointers only cares about addresses. The Fix Is Obvious Once You See The Bug If you want to compare values, return values: One * removed. Now alice.City() == bob.City() asks "is London equal to London?" and correctly answers true. Why Does This Pattern Exist At All? Fair question. Returning a pointer to a field isn't always wrong. There are legitimate reasons: Reason 1: You want the caller to be able to mutate the field. This is intentional mutability through a back-door. It's powerful. It's also a loaded gun pointed at your codebase's maintainability. Reason 2: You're working with large structs and want to avoid copies. If city were a massive struct (it isn't here), returning a pointer avoids copying it. Valid — but in practice, Go's compiler is smarter than most people give it credit for, and premature pointer optimization is a well-worn path to subtle bugs. Reason 3: You need to express "optional" / nullable. A *City can be nil. A City cannot. If the absence of a city is meaningful, a pointer communicates that. But *string and *int for nullable primitives should still make your eyes narrow — that's usually a job for a wrapper type or a dedicated Valid bool field. In Alice and Bob's case? None of these reasons apply. Returning &p.city here is a trap with no reward. The Smell Test Here's a rule of thumb worth keeping in your back pocket: If you're returning a pointer to a primitive, a string, or a simple value type — stop and ask why. Not "never do it." Just: why? What does the caller get from a *string that they wouldn't get from a string? If the answer isn't one of the three reasons above — mutability, avoiding large copies, or expressing nil — then you're probably handing someone a loaded footgun labeled "equality works normally here, trust me." The dangerous part isn't even the bug itself. The dangerous part is that it looks like it should work. alice.City() == bob.City() is perfectly valid Go. It compiles without complaint. The compiler isn't wrong — you can compare two *City values. It's just comparing the wrong thing. This is the category of bug where Go's type system can't save you, your tests might not catch it (because your test might use the same struct instance for both sides), and it sits quietly in production until someone notices that two users in the same city are being treated as if they're in different ones. One More Twist Here's where it gets truly devious. Consider this: Still false. Even though aliceCopy is a byte-for-byte copy of alice, it's a separate copy sitting at a different memory address. Their city fields are in different locations. And this: true! Because aliceRef.City() calls City() on the same underlying struct. Same struct, same field, same address. Pointers are about identity (where something lives), not equality (what it contains). Every time you see * in a return type, ask yourself which one the caller actually needs. The Moral Go doesn't hide what it's doing. *City in the return type is an honest signal: "I'm giving you an address, not a value." The language is telling you the truth. The trap is that we read code at a higher level of abstraction than the language executes it. We see alice.City() == bob.City() and our brain fills in "are they in the same city?" — a value comparison. But Go faithfully executes "are these two memory addresses identical?" — a pointer comparison. The code does exactly what it says. We just weren't reading carefully. So: return &field only when you mean it. Return values when you want value semantics. And when you see *string or *SomeSmallType in a return signature out in the wild, let your nose wrinkle — there's probably a story behind it, and it's rarely a happy one. If this saved you from a future production incident, share it with the Gopher in your life who deserves a heads up. 🐹

By Abhishek Kumar

One of Go's most misunderstood features I want to tell you about the day I stared at a timestamp bug for two hours. The logs made no sense. Two lines. Same function. The times were identical — even though one of them was supposed to fire 10 seconds later. I had sprinkled a defer in my code like a good little Gopher, expecting it to capture the world when it ran. But Go had other plans. That bug taught me something beautiful about how Go thinks. And once you see it, you cannot unsee it. The Code That Will Rewire Your Brain Quick — what does this print? Take a moment. Really think about it. ... Most engineers say: "The first timestamp, then 10 seconds later, the second timestamp." They are wrong. The actual output is two timestamps that are nearly identical — microseconds apart — even though the program takes 10 full seconds to finish. Why? The Rule That Changes Everything Here is the rule, and it is elegant in its simplicity: defer evaluates its arguments immediately. It only delays the call. Read that again. Slowly. When Go encounters defer fmt.Println(time.Now()), it does two things right then and there, before moving on to the next line: It evaluates time.Now() — captures the timestamp at that exact moment It says: "I'll call fmt.Println with this already-computed value when the function returns" The argument is frozen in time. It's like taking a photograph. The defer holds onto that photograph, not a live camera feed. So the timeline looks like this: The deferred Println runs at T+10, but it prints the value from T+0. The sleep is irrelevant to the value. It's already been decided. The Mental Model: Eager Arguments, Lazy Execution Think of defer as a reservation system. When you call defer f(x), Go immediately evaluates x, takes a note of the result, and books a reservation: "Call f with this exact value when the function exits." It's not saying: "At exit time, go figure out what x is." This distinction is everything. The value was locked in the moment defer was written. The future mutation of x is irrelevant. Where This Bites People (Real World Pain) The Logging Trap Wait — does this work? Let's think carefully. time.Since(start) is the argument to log.Printf. So it gets evaluated immediately, at the defer line, before any work is done. This would always log something like 127ns. This is a bug. The fix: By wrapping in an anonymous function, the entire function body is deferred — meaning time.Since(start) is now evaluated when the deferred func runs, not when it's declared. This is the idiomatic Go pattern for deferring logic that needs fresh values at exit time. The Loop Trap Here, each defer captures the value of i at the time of that iteration. This is actually correct behavior! Each iteration locks in its own value. The output is in reverse order (defers are LIFO — last in, first out), but each number is right. The Beautiful Duality of Defer There's a poetry to how defer works, once you understand it. It separates what from when. What to call, and with what arguments — decided now, at declaration time When to execute — decided later, at function exit This is a deliberate, thoughtful design choice. It means: You can reason about a defer's arguments locally, right where you wrote it, without needing to think about what values might look like at function exit. Resources are cleaned up with the context they were opened with. If you open a file and immediately defer file.Close(), the Close will always operate on that exact file handle, not some potentially-mutated version of a variable. Beautiful. Predictable. Safe. The Three Laws of Defer (Tattoo These On Your Brain) Law 1: Arguments are evaluated immediately. The value passed to a deferred function is computed at the defer statement, not at call time. Law 2: Deferred functions run LIFO. Last deferred = first to run. Like a stack. This is why cleanup code works elegantly: acquire A, acquire B, defer release B, defer release A. B is released before A. Perfect. Law 3: Deferred functions can read and modify named return values. This one is for another article, but know that a deferred function can affect what a function returns — if the return values are named. This is how some Go error wrapping patterns work. Why This Makes Go Special Languages with finally blocks (Java, Python, etc.) evaluate everything at execution time. You get fresh values, but the cleanup logic is separated from the resource acquisition — visually, conceptually, syntactically far away. Go's defer keeps cleanup right next to the thing being cleaned up: Two lines. Together. The relationship is obvious. The intent is clear. And because arguments are captured eagerly, you get a guarantee: the defer will always run with the values it saw at the moment of its declaration, unaffected by everything that happens afterward. That's not a quirk. That's a feature. That's Go being honest with you about what it promises to do. The Takeaway Next time you write defer, ask yourself: "Are any of these arguments something I want evaluated NOW versus at exit time?" If you want NOW: pass it directly. defer f(x) — x is captured immediately. If you want LATER: wrap it. defer func() { f(x) }() — x is evaluated when the deferred function runs. One mental model. Two clear patterns. Zero surprises. A Note of Appreciation I love Go for moments like this. The language has opinions. It makes choices that feel strange at first, then feel right once you understand the reasoning. Defer is not broken. Defer is not confusing once you know the rule. Defer is consistent — a quality more valuable in a programming language than almost anything else. Go isn't trying to protect you from yourself with magic. It's giving you a clear, inspectable mental model and trusting you to use it well. That's the Go philosophy. And that's why, after all these years, I still wake up excited to write it. If this rewired something in your brain, share it. Every Go engineer deserves to learn this before it bites them in production — not after. Happy coding. Keep reading the spec. 🐹

  Beware of Fake KYC Update Requests 
	

Fraudsters are posing as Bank officials 
to misuse your Banking Details 
	
	
	
	

	
	
	
	

Dear HDFC Bank Customer, 

Fraudsters are posing as bank officials via SMS, WhatsApp, or calls. 
They claim your account will be blocked unless RE-KYC is completed , and send a link to update your details. 

This link opens a fake app or site. Any information entered can be misused to access your Bank Account or make fraudulent transactions. 
Sharing such details can put your account at serious risk. 

Stay Alert! 
To protect yourself from Re-KYC fraud, follow these simple rules: 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Don’t act on unknown KYC update requests. Contact your Bank or visit a Branch to confirm. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Never download any app or file from suspicious or unverified sources. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

The Bank will never ask for your account details, passwords, or OTPs via call, SMS, or email. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Report suspicious calls or messages on the Chakshu portal at  https://t13.mailers.hdfcbank.bank.in/r/?id=t972fcb3a-a24b-4074-b769-b7825ef36736,236a7c,a6564 sancharsaathi.gov.in  or via the Sanchar Saathi app. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

If you’ve fallen victim to such fraud, immediately contact your bank. 

You can also file a complaint at  https://t13.mailers.hdfcbank.bank.in/r/?id=t972fcb3a-a24b-4074-b769-b7825ef36736,236a7c,a6565 cybercrime.gov.in  or call 1930.

Channels don't just pass data — they pass time.

Golang: The Random Chapters

By Abhishek Kumar


By Abhishek Kumar

    
    
    Read this article on LinkedIn to join the conversation
Read on LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/go-memory-model-bulb-moment-channels-dont-just-pass-data-kumar-ogcnc?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3Bp6h%2BbyqDRYO1gkgqvYahQQ%3D%3D&midToken=AQEIM4HzHiyK2w&midSig=0LZUKARFPMuc81&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-ghmp60~mlqjvdgd~gp-null-null&eid=ghmp60-mlqjvdgd-gp
  
I used to think Go channels were just typed queues — a neat way to move values between goroutines. Then I stumbled onto the Go Memory Model's channel guarantees and had a full stop, re-read-it-twice moment. An unbuffered channel isn't just sending a value. It's creating a hard synchronization point — a moment where one goroutine can't move forward until the other shows up. That handshake also orders everything that happened before it. sync_demo.go 🔑 The rule: In an unbuffered channel, the nth receive happens-before the nth send completes — and vice versa. Both goroutines see all writes the other made before the handshake. The channel is a time contract, not just a pipe. This is why the panics are genuinely, provably impossible — not just unlikely. The Go Memory Model gives you an iron guarantee. You don't need mutexes here. The channel is the lock. Next time you reach for a out of habit — ask yourself: is there a channel handshake I could lean on instead?

​
The market is tough.

Layoffs. Hiring freezes. Fewer openings.
You’re not imagining it.

But here’s the uncomfortable part:

Ranting about it won’t move your career forward.

Rewriting your resume will.

I’ve been watching smart, capable professionals spiral into
frustration lately:

• “No one’s hiring.”
• “I don’t have enough experience.”
• “My last manager ruined my growth.”

And while those feelings are valid… they’re not leverage.

The candidates getting interviews right now aren’t the calmest
ones.

They’re the ones who convert frustration into better positioning.

Let’s talk about how to actually do that this week.

----------------------------------
1. Translate complaints into proof
----------------------------------

Every frustration hides a result.

You think:
“I didn’t get real ownership.”

What that often means:
You handled ambiguity.
You filled gaps.
You solved problems no one else wanted.

Your resume should show that.

Instead of:
“Supported product launch initiatives”

Write:
“Coordinated cross-functional product launch across design,
engineering, and marketing, contributing to on-time release for
50K+ users.”

Ownership isn’t about title.
It’s about impact.

In our resume review sessions (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/lmu9dwkn03smhnewlgqa6h8vvmv00cgh7wmzo/g3hk7npns5hmrkm5dpur/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
) inside the accelerator, this is usually the biggest shift we
make: turning passive language into ownership language.

Most people have more proof than they think. It’s just buried
under safe wording.

------------------------------------------------
2. Let rejection feedback sharpen your narrative
------------------------------------------------

If you’ve heard:
“Not enough leadership.”

That’s not always about your experience.

It’s often about how you’re framing it.

Compare these:

“5 years of experience in analytics”

vs.

“Data analyst who partnered with product and engineering to
improve retention by 18% and mentored 2 junior analysts”

Same person. Different story.

Recruiters don’t hire years. They hire signals.

Every rejection contains information.
The mistake is ignoring it.

Inside our office hours (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/lmu9dwkn03smhnewlgqa6h8vvmv00cgh7wmzo/g3hk7npns5hmrkm5dpur/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
), we dissect these signals live. Sometimes it’s not a skills
gap. It’s a clarity gap.

-----------------------------------------------------------
3. Rebuild one role per day (stop waiting for perfect time)
-----------------------------------------------------------

Most professionals treat resume rewriting like a “weekend
project.”

That’s how it never gets done.

Instead:

* Monday: Rewrite your current role
* Tuesday: Add metrics to your previous one
* Wednesday: Tighten your summary
* Thursday: Align keywords with 3 active roles
* Friday: Remove fluff and vague language

Small iterations compound.

Progress beats the fantasy of a flawless resume.

-----------------------------------
4. Remove emotion. Insert outcomes.
-----------------------------------

This is where most resumes collapse.

You might feel:
“I was stuck in chaos.”
“I had no support.”
“It was political.”

That may be true.

But your resume is not a journal.

Instead of:
“Worked in a fast-paced, high-pressure environment”

Write:
“Managed 8 simultaneous initiatives across marketing and
engineering teams, delivering all milestones within deadline
despite shifting priorities.”

One shows frustration.
One shows resilience.

Hiring managers don’t reward struggle.
They reward outcomes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
5. Stop sounding like a participant. Start sounding like a
driver.
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Many resumes read like this:

• Helped with
• Assisted in
• Supported
• Contributed to

Those words signal low ownership.

Replace them with:

• Led
• Built
• Designed
• Launched
• Improved
• Reduced
• Scaled

Even if you weren’t the only person involved.

The goal is accuracy with confidence.

Average candidates complain about the market.

Strong candidates adapt to it.

And the adaptation usually starts with rewriting how they present
themselves.

The job market isn’t fair.
But it is responsive.

Clearer positioning → higher visibility → more interviews.

That’s predictable.

And if you want structured help with that positioning - resume
rewrites, accountability, feedback loops, and community sessions
where we refine this together - that’s exactly why the Job
Hunting Accelerator (

) exists.

Not to motivate you. To tighten your execution.

Your frustration is real. Channel it. Rewrite one role tonight.

Yudi here.

I regularly bring immigration lawyers from Manifest Law on my
weekly YT live sessions to talk about visas, jobs, and long-term

community.

​

I work closely with their team and trust their lawyers,
especially because they understand the real situations students
and working professionals face in the US.

​

They’ve also agreed to offer a free legal consultation for
